To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) dykeland removal is likely to be controversial, 2) dykeland restoration is likely to be more acceptable than dykeland removal, 3) the most common discourse is pro-dykelands for cultural reasons, 4) there is little support for wetland restoration, even for flood mitigation, and 5) the two minority viewpoints were concerned with governance.

dykeland maintenance is preferred over wetland restoration by the dominant discourse in the Acadian dykes of Nova Scotia, which is characterized by women, dykelands users and local residents, and is likely resistant to change.
the dykelands of the Bay of Fundy are a cultural landscape that has been maintained by a local agricultural sector that is no longer economically viable.

the social limits to coastal adaptation in new-world cultural landscapes, and the governance arrangements that can overcome these limits.
the governance of cultural landscapes, which are often under-researched and poorly understood.
the governance of adaptation, and the need for a more nuanced approach to the management of cultural landscapes, and their adaptation to climate change.

the Acadian dyke system has become a cultural icon, and the dominant public discourse is that it should be maintained, but that there are some who would prefer to see wetland restoration, especially if it were to be done in a way that is not detrimental to local farming interests.
the Acadian dykelsands of Nova Scotia are a cultural agricultural landscape with a high degree of social and governance complexity.
the dykelands are in need of restoration and maintenance to 2050, but this will require a shift in the dominant discourse and governance arrangements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
climate adaptation in new-world cultural landscapes is likely to be difficult, and will be shaped by a range of social and institutional barriers.

climate change adaptation planning in new world cultural landscapes is a complex and difficult process, and that it is important to understand the discourses that are emerging, and how to engage them.
dykeland management is a social problem with a complex set of social and political constraints, and that the dykelands are a social problem that requires more than technical expertise to solve.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cultural landscapes are not always the ‘natural’ choice for adaptation, and that cultural landscapes may not be as resilient as their proponents believe.
dykeland removal will be a difficult sell, even to dykeland advocates, unless the benefits of wetland restoration can be framed in terms of flood mitigation and not just cost-saving.
the cultural agricultural landscape of dykelands in the Bay of Fundy is highly valued, but that the governance arrangements for managing dykelands are poorly suited to adaptation to climate change.
